title: 2026 midterm elections: The biggest takeaways | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Ahistoric Democratic waveswept the party into power in Congress and in statehousesacross the countryon Tuesday, as voters rebuked President Donald Trump and rejected the candidates he’d propped up in key races.

In an election in which Trump urged his faithful to vote like he was on the ballot, Republicans were washed out of power in places the party hadn’t lost in a generation — and sometimes more. Democrats won a Senate race in Kansas for the first time since the 1930s; a Senate seat in South Carolina that they’d lost when Strom Thurmond switched parties in the 1960s; and a slew of statewide offices in Texas, where they hadn’t won any since the 1990s.

The gains the GOP had made during the Trump era, particularly among Latinos and in rural areas, were wiped out in a single night.

And after a decade of dismal showings in the Rust Belt and Great Plains, the Democratic Party roared back to life in Middle America. The party won both the governor’s office and a Senate race in each of Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota and Ohio. It won House races in districts Trump won by 20 percentage points just two years ago and toppled GOP state legislative supermajorities in states like Indiana and Missouri. And Democrats entrenched in statehouses a new generation of potential political stars who now have opportunities to build on the Democratic gains in their states — in figures like Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand and Indiana Secretary of State-elect Beau Bayh.

Though the White House is already deflecting blame, the results were a visceral rejection of Trump’s actions in his second term. And across the map, there was a long list of examples of races in which the president’s own recruiting efforts and endorsements had backfired.

Candidates who had aligned themselves with the president and mimicked Trump’s approach to controversy, like Vivek Ramaswamy in the Ohio governor’s race and Ken Paxton in the Texas Senate race, lost. So did hardline conservatives he chose over more moderate contenders, like Rep. Mike Collins in the Georgia Senate race.

His redistricting gambit, a bid to redraw red states’ congressional maps to solidify the GOP’s narrow House majority, also fell flat, with Democrats winning a number of seats even after Republicans had changed the maps to limit their odds of doing so.

As votes continue to be counted, Democrats have a number of opportunities to build on a historic night – leading in several competitive Senate races in which the outcome is too early to call.

Here are takeaways from the 2026 midterm elections:

No state illustrated the dramatic Democratic wave more than Texas.

The state had not elected a Democrat to statewide office in over three decades, and Democrats had gotten their hopes up before — only to suffer devastating defeat.

But the dam broke on Tuesday. Democrat James Talarico won the high-profile open Senate race, but in an even more striking result, Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s race, defeating three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Abbott entered the race with massive advantages, including a war chest of over $100 million. He was vying for a chance to become the state’s longest-serving governor after a political career that began in the 1990s.

Other Republican statewide officials were trailing in their races, including Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, the presiding officer of the state Senate.

Taken together, the results augur profound change in a state that has long been known as the biggest Republican stronghold in the country.

Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats the party needed to claim the majority, winning races in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas — and doing so by defeating several candidates who were hand-picked by Trump.

The party also retained all of its Senate seats. in a closely watched contest in Michigan, progressive former public health official Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan held off former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya in Minnesota.

The Senate race in Mississippi, which Trump won by 23 points just two years ago, was yet to be decided, with Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith separated by a razor-thin margin.

Talarico ushered in a generational moment for Texas Democrats as he defeated Paxton, the scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general who was endorsed by Trump, in what became the most expensive Senate race in US history.

In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson ousted five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins, a moderate in a blue state who Democrats had nevertheless fallen short of defeating several times.

In Kansas, megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Sen. Roger Marshall – the latest reminder that though it’s barn-red at the presidential level, voters in the state are willing to elect Democrats.

In Iowa, state lawmaker Josh Turek defeated Rep. Ashley Hinson — one of the GOP’s star recruits of the 2026 cycle — in the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. Turek made the case that the state was bearing the brunt of Trump’s tariffs and high diesel prices resulting from the war with Iran.

In Ohio, two years after losing the state’s other Senate seat, Democrat Sherrod Brown completed a political comeback by defeating Republican Sen. Jon Husted.

And in North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper trounced former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley — an outcome that was widely expected by strategists in both parties.

South Carolina, though, was a stunner. Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham — claiming a seat that’s been in GOP hands since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964. Fritz Hollings in 1998 was the last Democrat to win a Senate seat in South Carolina.

A roster of South Carolina political veterans had been interested in running for the seat after Lindsey Graham’s death in July. But Trump asked Graham’s sister — a political novice — first to occupy the seat temporarily and later pressured her to run for a full term. She struggled in debates and on the campaign trail.

Republicans sought to get an early advantage in the midterms byredrawing a slew of House districts in red statesto pick up more seats.

By most accounts, the strategy backfired.

Democrats will maintain control of at least eight of the 15 districts targeted by GOP redistricting efforts and have flipped at least four seats away from Republicans, according to CNN projections.

So far, they’ve held on to three targeted seats in Florida, two in Texas, and one each in Ohio, Alabama and North Carolina. Meanwhile, Democrats have so far picked up three seats in California and one in Utah.

In Texas, Democrats were on track to win most of the five seats that Republicans reconfigured to help themselves.

Among the striking examples was in the 34th Congressional District in South Texas. GOP state lawmakers redrew the seat to be one that Trump would have carried by 10 percentage points, but Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez was winning it by double digits by early Wednesday.

In Alabama, one of the biggest targets of the Republican redistricting campaign, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures, held on, despite being drawn into a district that Trump would have carried by 14 percentage points two years ago.

“We have crushed the Republican gerrymander all across the land,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is now on the path to become thefirst Black speaker of the House, said on X.

The political environment might have wiped Republicans out anyway. But a series of GOP recruiting missteps — largely on Trump’s part — appear to have worsened the party’s problems on Tuesday.

Bungling South Carolina only came after Lindsey Graham’s unexpected death. But Texas was a trainwreck two years in the making for the GOP.

Trump ignored Republicans who spent months lobbying him to endorse the more moderate incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, and help him ward off a primary challenge from Paxton. He stayed out of the primary, and then, after Cornyn and Paxton advanced to a runoff, he endorsed Paxton — effectively guaranteeing his victory and saddling the party with a nominee who was a lackadaisical campaigner, poor fundraiser and easy target, after decades of scandals.

Georgia Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff’s easy reelection win was another example of Trump’s failed midterm maneuvering: His endorsement boosted Rep. Mike Collins to a primary win over a more moderate alternative, former football coach Derek Dooley, backed by popular two-term Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Ossoff’s strengths and Collins’ struggles — and histies to White nationalistshighlighted frequently by the Democrat — affected the governor’s race in Georgia as well. Keisha Lance Bottoms is now set to become the nation’s first Black female governor.

Trump effectively cleared the field in Ohio for Vivek Ramaswamy, who won the president’s favor in part because he was Trump’s only defender in the 2024 GOP presidential debates that Trump skipped.

But Ramaswamy’s decision to air an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, backfired. And rather than encouraging Ramaswamy to take it off the air, both Trump and Vice President JD Vance doubled down, defending its contents. Trump said he would have used an ad like it, too. However, interviews with a number of independent and Republican voters in Ohio revealed widespread disgust with Ramaswamy’s move — which culminated Tuesday in Acton’s victory.

Tech mogul Elon Musk poured $168 million into two Texas super PACs aimed at salvaging Paxton’s bid for the Senate and helping the GOP retain its majority in the chamber.

“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Talarico said in his victory speech.

Musk also devoted millions more to voter outreach in Texas, through his own political group, America PAC, and contributed more than $5 million to Abbott’s reelection campaign.

Overall, Musk has pumped nearlyhalf a billion dollarsinto federal committees in this election cycle to become the country’s largest publicly disclosed political donor.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk wrote overnight on X, the platform he purchased and renamed from Twitter.

Trump watched returns come in from the White House East Room, where the mood was described as tense. Notably, he went silent on Truth Social for three hours Tuesday night as Democrats kept winning races before posting just after 10:30 p.m.: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

The stunning results across a swath of America were not primarily the fault of the Iran war he began eight months ago — he told the Wall Street Journal that was only a “piece” of it — or the tariffs that drove up prices or his fixation on topics far from voters’ minds, Trump insisted.

It was the candidates who were to blame, he argued, helped along by favorable coverage of Democrats on his once-favorite channel, Fox News. The results were only a “little surprise,” he would later tell that channel. The winds of history were always against him, he’d long warned. He neglected to mention that he had selected many of the candidates himself.

“I thought they’d do better,” he told Fox, referring to Republicans in the third person rather than the party he is currently leading. Later, he attributed the losses to a “mood in the air.”

He also insisted Tuesday night that his governing agenda would continue apace, despite the dramatically altered political conditions in Washington.

“But I don’t view it as a hit on me,” Trump told Fox News in a live phone interview. “We’ve had the greatest two years in the history of the presidency in terms of the economy, in terms of all the things that we’ve done.”

In Florida, the results offered evidence of a potentially enormous swing among Latino voters in Democrats’ favor.

Democrats held onto three seats that Republicans had redrawn in an effort to guarantee victories this fall. CNN has projected that Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz will win in redrawn districts, as will Democrat Pia Dandiya in the 22nd District.

In another heavily Hispanic district in central Florida the GOP had redrawn, Democratic Rep. Darren Soto narrowly leads his Republican challenger in the 9th District.

But the biggest eye-opener might come in South Florida’s 27th District, which is based in the overwhelmingly Latino Miami-Dade County.

Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar won by 20 percentage points two years ago. She might hold on this year — but she led Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez by just over a thousand votes as of early Wednesday morning. A swing of that size means the gains Trump made with Latino voters in 2024 have effectively evaporated, at least in Florida.

The results were full of encouraging signs for Democrats who may want to run for president in 2028.

At least two potential White House contenders, Govs. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, cruised to victory in their reelection bids. Pritzker nodded to speculation about his political future in his victory speech, saying he’s been asked, “What’s next?”

“The answer is simple: I’m going to ask you to continue to hope, to wrap yourself in hope, in courage,” Pritzker said. “We climbed one mountain tonight, but we are sitting at the base of another.”

Another possible White House contender, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, was not on the ballot Tuesday but scored a big win when his former aide, Zach Dembo, flipped a GOP-friendly House district in central Kentucky.

And in Georgia, Ossoff’s decisive victory is likely to increase 2028 buzz surrounding him, even if he has denied interest in running. Bottoms winning the governor’s race means a fellow Democrat would pick his replacement in the Senate if he were to vacate his seat for a presidential run.

Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly was also among potential presidential candidates celebrating the results. But in a late-night call with reporters, he declined to say whether the results made him more inclined to run in 2028, saying, “I don’t think of it in that context.”

“I think of it as a big win for the American people,” Kelly said.

Before this year, only three Black candidates had ever won governor’s races in the United States — and multiple Black governors had never served simultaneously. Those ranks are rapidly growing, with four Black candidates winning Tuesday and several more running in races that have not yet been decided.

In Georgia, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any state in United States history when she became the first Democrat to win the office in 28 years.

In Florida, Rep. Byron Donalds became the first Black Republican elected governor in United States history.

In Wisconsin, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a Democrat, won the race to replace outgoing Gov. Tony Evers in the marquee presidential battleground state.

And Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat, won a second term.

Their wins were part of aseries of historic firstsin this year’s midterms.

Several of those firsts occurred in Senate races. In New Hampshire, Rep. Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. And Annie Andrews is projected to become the first elected female US senator from South Carolina. In Michigan, El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

Democrat Deb Haaland, meanwhile, became the first Native American woman to win a race for governor with her victory in New Mexico.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN’s Fredreka Schouten contributed to this report.
